items.prompt: Define a scalar quantity, giving ONE example.
items.answer: A scalar quantity is a physical quantity that has only magnitude (size), with no associated direction. Example: mass, distance, speed or time.
items.explanation: Because a scalar has no direction, scalar quantities are combined using ordinary arithmetic (simple addition and subtraction), unlike vector quantities.

items.prompt: Define a vector quantity, giving ONE example.
items.answer: A vector quantity is a physical quantity that has both magnitude and direction. Example: force, displacement, velocity or acceleration.
items.explanation: A vector must always be stated with both a size and a direction (e.g. "5 m east") to be fully and correctly specified.

items.context: Vectors acting along the same straight line may be added algebraically, taking direction into account using a sign convention (e.g. right = positive, left = negative).
items.prompt: Two forces act on the same object along the same straight line: 25 N to the right and 10 N to the left. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the resultant force.
items.answer: Resultant = 15 N to the right.
items.explanation: Taking right as positive: Fnet = 25 + (−10) = 15 N. Since the result is positive, the resultant force is 15 N to the right.

items.context: For two vectors acting at right angles to each other: R = √(F₁² + F₂²); tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent
items.prompt: Two forces, 9 N and 12 N, act at right angles to each other on the same point. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force, and the angle the resultant makes with the 9 N force.
items.answer: R = 15 N, at 53.13° to the 9 N force.

items.context: Distance is a scalar quantity (the total length of the path travelled); displacement is a vector quantity (the straight-line distance and direction from the starting point to the end point).
items.prompt: A hiker walks 80 m due east, then 60 m due north. Calculate (a) the total distance walked by the hiker, and (b) the magnitude of the hiker’s resultant displacement.
items.explanation: (a) Distance is simply the sum of the path lengths: 80 + 60 = 140 m. (b) Displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish; since the two legs are perpendicular, it is found using Pythagoras: √(80² + 60²) = √(6400 + 3600) = √10000 = 100 m. Note that the 100 m displacement is smaller than the 140 m distance, illustrating the difference between the two quantities.

items.prompt: Distinguish between speed and velocity.
items.answer: Speed is a scalar quantity equal to the rate of change of distance (distance travelled per unit time). Velocity is a vector quantity equal to the rate of change of displacement (displacement per unit time, in a stated direction).
items.explanation: Because velocity includes direction, an object moving at constant speed around a curved path (where its direction keeps changing) does not have a constant velocity.

items.prompt: Define acceleration.
items.answer: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity of an object, i.e. the change in velocity per unit time. It is a vector quantity.
items.explanation: An object accelerates whenever its speed changes, its direction of motion changes, or both — a change in either component of velocity constitutes an acceleration.

items.context: v = u + at
items.prompt: A car travelling at 5 m·s⁻¹ accelerates uniformly at 2 m·s⁻² for 4 s. Calculate the car’s final velocity.
items.answer: v = 13 m·s⁻¹

items.context: s = ut + ½at²
items.prompt: A ball moving along a straight track has an initial velocity of 10 m·s⁻¹ and undergoes a uniform acceleration of 3 m·s⁻² for 5 s. Calculate the ball’s displacement during this time.

items.context: v² = u² + 2as
items.prompt: A car travelling at 30 m·s⁻¹ applies its brakes and comes to rest after travelling a further 75 m. Calculate the car’s (uniform) acceleration while braking.
items.answer: a = −6 m·s⁻² (i.e. a deceleration of 6 m·s⁻²)
items.explanation: v² = u² + 2as → 0² = 30² + 2 × a × 75 → 0 = 900 + 150a → a = −900 ÷ 150 = −6 m·s⁻². The negative sign shows the acceleration acts opposite to the direction of motion, i.e. the car is decelerating.

items.context: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at² (acceleration phase); s = vt (constant-velocity phase)
items.prompt: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2.5 m·s⁻² for 6 s. It then travels at the velocity it has reached for a further 10 s at constant velocity. Calculate (a) the velocity reached at the end of the acceleration phase, and (b) the total distance travelled during the full 16 s.
items.answer: (a) v = 15 m·s⁻¹  (b) total distance = 195 m
items.explanation: (a) v = u + at = 0 + (2.5 × 6) = 15 m·s⁻¹. (b) Distance during acceleration: s₁ = ut + ½at² = 0 + (½ × 2.5 × 6²) = 45 m. Distance during constant velocity: s₂ = vt = 15 × 10 = 150 m. Total distance = s₁ + s₂ = 45 + 150 = 195 m.

items.context: On a velocity-time graph, acceleration = gradient of the graph, and distance travelled = area under the graph.
items.prompt: A velocity-time graph shows an object accelerating uniformly from 4 m·s⁻¹ to 16 m·s⁻¹ over the first 6 s, and then travelling at a constant 16 m·s⁻¹ for a further 4 s. Calculate (a) the object’s acceleration during the first 6 s, and (b) the total distance travelled over the full 10 s, using the area under the graph.
items.answer: (a) a = 2 m·s⁻²  (b) total distance = 124 m
items.explanation: (a) a = (v − u) ÷ t = (16 − 4) ÷ 6 = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 m·s⁻². (b) Distance for the first 6 s (a trapezium under the graph) = ½ × (4 + 16) × 6 = 60 m. Distance for the last 4 s (a rectangle, since velocity is constant) = 16 × 4 = 64 m. Total distance = 60 + 64 = 124 m.

items.prompt: Define gravitational potential energy.
items.answer: Gravitational potential energy is the energy an object possesses due to its position (height) above a chosen reference point, within a gravitational field.
items.explanation: Gravitational potential energy is calculated using Ep = mgh, where h is the height above the chosen reference level.

items.prompt: State the law of conservation of mechanical energy.
items.answer: In the absence of friction (or any other non-conservative force), the total mechanical energy of a system — the sum of its kinetic energy and its gravitational potential energy — remains constant.
items.explanation: This can be written as Ek + Ep = constant, meaning that any loss in potential energy is exactly balanced by an equal gain in kinetic energy, and vice versa, provided no energy is lost to friction or air resistance.

items.context: Ep = mgh; g = 9.8 m·s⁻²
items.prompt: Calculate the gravitational potential energy of a 2 kg object held 5 m above the ground.
items.answer: Ep = 98 J

items.context: Ek = ½mv²
items.prompt: A 4 kg trolley moves at 6 m·s⁻¹. Calculate (a) its kinetic energy, and (b) its new kinetic energy if its speed doubles to 12 m·s⁻¹.
items.answer: (a) Ek = 72 J  (b) Ek = 288 J
items.explanation: (a) Ek = ½mv² = ½ × 4 × 6² = ½ × 4 × 36 = 72 J. (b) Ek = ½ × 4 × 12² = ½ × 4 × 144 = 288 J. Note that doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large (288 ÷ 72 = 4), since Ek is proportional to v².

items.context: Conservation of mechanical energy (no air resistance): mgh = ½mv² → v = √(2gh)
items.prompt: An object is released from rest and falls freely from a height of 20 m. Ignoring air resistance, use the principle of conservation of mechanical energy to calculate the object’s speed just before it strikes the ground.
items.explanation: All of the object’s initial gravitational potential energy converts to kinetic energy by the time it lands: mgh = ½mv² → v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 20) = √392 ≈ 19.80 m·s⁻¹. Note that the mass cancels out, so the final speed does not depend on the mass of the object.

items.prompt: A hiker argues that taking a long zigzag path up a hill requires more energy against gravity than climbing straight up, "because you walk much further". Evaluate the hiker's reasoning, treating the walking itself as frictionless.
items.answer: The work done against GRAVITY is identical, because gravitational potential energy depends only on the change in height.
items.explanation: Ep = mgh contains the vertical height and nothing else — not the distance walked, not the route, not the steepness. Gravity is a conservative force, which means precisely that the work done against it between two points is independent of the path taken; a 70 kg hiker climbing 400 m does 70 × 9.8 × 400 ≈ 274 kJ against gravity by any route. On the zigzag, the force needed at each step is smaller because the slope is gentler, and the distance is correspondingly longer, and the product is unchanged. Real hikers are right that the zigzag is easier and wrong about why: it is easier because it demands less force at any moment, not less energy overall. Outside this question's frictionless idealisation the longer path does cost extra in friction and in the inefficiency of human muscle, which is a separate account from the work against gravity.

items.prompt: Define the amplitude of a transverse wave.
items.answer: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle of the medium from its equilibrium (rest) position.
items.explanation: A larger amplitude means the particles of the medium move further from their rest position, which for many waves corresponds to a wave carrying more energy.

items.prompt: Define the wavelength of a transverse wave.
items.answer: Wavelength is the distance between any two successive points on a wave that are in phase with each other, for example between two successive crests or two successive troughs.
items.explanation: Wavelength is usually represented by the symbol λ and measured in metres.

items.context: v = fλ; T = 1 ÷ f
items.prompt: A transverse wave has a wavelength of 0.4 m and travels at a speed of 20 m·s⁻¹. Calculate (a) the frequency of the wave, and (b) its period.
A learner claims a pulse slows down as it travels along a rope, "because it loses energy on the way, and something with less energy moves more slowly". Evaluate this claim.
items.answer: The claim is wrong in its conclusion, though a real pulse does fade. Losing energy reduces a pulse's amplitude, not its speed.
items.explanation: A pulse on a real rope does lose energy, to internal friction within the rope and to the air, so it grows visibly smaller as it travels — the learner has noticed something real. Speed is a different matter: it is fixed by the rope's tension and mass per unit length, v = √(T ÷ µ), and neither changes as the pulse passes. So the pulse fades without slowing, arriving at the far end at the same moment a stronger pulse would, only smaller. The reasoning applied here belongs to objects, where Ek = ½mv² ties energy to speed directly. For a wave, energy is tied to AMPLITUDE and speed to the medium, and keeping those two attachments straight is what the question is testing. Tightening the rope would genuinely speed the pulse up, without anyone adding energy to the pulse itself.

items.context: Principle of superposition: when two or more pulses meet, the resultant displacement of the medium at any point is the sum of the individual displacements of each pulse at that point.
items.prompt: State the principle of superposition of waves. Two pulses travelling in the same medium meet at a point: pulse A has an amplitude of 5 cm upward, and pulse B has an amplitude of 3 cm downward. Calculate the resultant displacement of the medium at the point where the two pulses fully overlap, and state whether this is an example of constructive or destructive interference.
items.answer: Principle stated above; resultant displacement = 2 cm upward; this is destructive interference.
items.explanation: Taking upward as positive: resultant = 5 + (−3) = 2 cm upward. Because the resultant amplitude (2 cm) is smaller than the larger of the two individual pulses (5 cm) — the pulses partly cancel each other out — this is destructive interference, rather than constructive interference (which would occur if the pulses reinforced each other, e.g. if both were upward).

items.prompt: Define a longitudinal wave.
items.answer: A longitudinal wave is a wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate parallel to (along the same line as) the direction in which the wave travels.
items.explanation: This is in contrast to a transverse wave, in which the particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave travel.

items.prompt: Define a compression and a rarefaction in a longitudinal wave.
items.answer: A compression is a region of a longitudinal wave where the particles of the medium are pushed close together (a region of higher density/pressure). A rarefaction is a region where the particles are spread further apart than normal (a region of lower density/pressure).
items.explanation: Compressions and rarefactions alternate along a longitudinal wave; the distance between two successive compressions (or two successive rarefactions) is equal to one wavelength.

items.prompt: Distinguish between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave in terms of the direction in which the particles of the medium vibrate, relative to the direction of wave propagation, giving ONE example of each.
items.answer: In a transverse wave, the particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave travel (e.g. a wave on a string, or light). In a longitudinal wave, the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of wave travel (e.g. a sound wave, or a compression wave in a spring).
items.explanation: This difference in vibration direction is the defining distinction between the two wave types, and determines how compressions/rarefactions (longitudinal) or crests/troughs (transverse) are formed.

items.context: f = 1 ÷ T; v = fλ
items.prompt: A longitudinal wave is produced with a period of 0.5 s and a wavelength of 1.5 m. Calculate (a) the frequency of the wave, and (b) the speed at which the wave travels.
items.answer: (a) f = 2 Hz  (b) v = 3 m·s⁻¹

items.context: For a longitudinal wave, the distance between two adjacent compressions equals one wavelength. T = total time ÷ number of waves; f = 1 ÷ T; v = fλ
items.prompt: A vibrating source produces a longitudinal wave along a spring; adjacent compressions in the spring are found to be 0.8 m apart. The source takes 3.2 s to produce 8 complete waves. Calculate (a) the period of the wave, (b) the frequency of the wave, and (c) the speed at which the wave travels along the spring.
items.explanation: (a) T = total time ÷ number of waves = 3.2 ÷ 8 = 0.4 s. (b) f = 1 ÷ T = 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5 Hz. (c) The 0.8 m spacing between adjacent compressions is the wavelength, so v = fλ = 2.5 × 0.8 = 2.0 m·s⁻¹.

items.prompt: Give TWO examples of longitudinal waves, and state whether the particles of the medium vibrate parallel or perpendicular to the direction the wave travels.
items.answer: Examples: sound waves, and compression waves in a spring/slinky (seismic P-waves are also acceptable). The particles vibrate parallel to the direction the wave travels.
items.explanation: Sound is the most common everyday example of a longitudinal wave, transmitted through a medium (such as air) as a series of compressions and rarefactions.

items.prompt: Define the pitch of a sound, and state which property of a sound wave determines it.
items.answer: Pitch is how high or low a sound is perceived to be. It is determined by the frequency of the sound wave — a higher frequency produces a higher pitch.
items.explanation: For example, a note played on a small, tightly-strung instrument typically has a higher frequency, and so a higher pitch, than a note played on a large, loosely-strung one.

items.prompt: Define the loudness of a sound, and state which property of a sound wave determines it.
items.answer: Loudness is how loud or soft a sound is perceived to be. It is determined by the amplitude of the sound wave — a larger amplitude produces a louder sound.
items.explanation: A larger amplitude corresponds to a sound wave carrying more energy, which is perceived by the ear as being louder.

items.context: distance = (speed × time) ÷ 2, for an echo, since the sound travels to the reflecting surface and back
items.prompt: A person shouts toward a distant cliff face and hears the echo of their shout 1.8 s later. If the speed of sound in air is 340 m·s⁻¹, calculate the distance between the person and the cliff face.
items.answer: distance = 306 m
items.explanation: The 1.8 s is the time for the sound to travel to the cliff AND back, so the one-way distance is: d = (v × t) ÷ 2 = (340 × 1.8) ÷ 2 = 612 ÷ 2 = 306 m.

items.context: v = fλ
items.prompt: A sound wave of frequency 256 Hz (the musical note middle C) travels through air at a speed of 340 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the wavelength of this sound wave.

items.context: depth = ½ × v × t
items.prompt: A ship's sonar gives a depth reading that is consistently too large in one part of a bay. The operator blames a faulty timer. A colleague suggests the water there is colder than the value of v the instrument assumes. Whose reasoning better explains a reading that is too LARGE? Justify your answer.
items.answer: Neither, as stated — colder water would make the reading too SMALL. A timer fault is possible, and warmer water fits the observation better.
items.explanation: The instrument computes depth = ½ × v × t using an assumed speed of sound, and reports too large a depth if either t is measured too long or the true v exceeds the assumed one. Sound travels faster in warmer water, roughly 4 m·s⁻¹ for each degree Celsius, so water WARMER than assumed makes the pulse return sooner than expected — but the instrument multiplies the true, shorter time by the smaller assumed speed and therefore underestimates. Working it through the other way: colder water slows the pulse, the echo takes longer, and the instrument reads too DEEP. So the colleague has identified the right mechanism and named the wrong direction, and their explanation works once corrected to colder water. The operator's timer fault also fits and is the less likely of the two, being testable by sounding a known depth elsewhere in the bay.

items.prompt: Define electromagnetic radiation.
items.answer: Electromagnetic radiation consists of transverse waves made up of oscillating, mutually perpendicular electric and magnetic fields, which require no medium to travel through and move at the speed of light in a vacuum.
items.explanation: Because electromagnetic waves need no medium, they are able to travel through the vacuum of space, unlike mechanical waves such as sound.

items.context: The electromagnetic spectrum, in order of increasing frequency: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
items.prompt: Arrange the following regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of INCREASING frequency: visible light, radio waves, gamma rays, ultraviolet radiation.
items.answer: radio waves, visible light, ultraviolet radiation, gamma rays
items.explanation: All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed (c) in a vacuum, and since c = fλ is constant, frequency increases as wavelength decreases across the spectrum: radio waves have the lowest frequency (longest wavelength) of the four, followed by visible light, then ultraviolet, with gamma rays having the highest frequency (shortest wavelength).

items.context: c = fλ; c = 3 × 10⁸ m·s⁻¹
items.prompt: Calculate the frequency of a beam of light with a wavelength of 500 nm (5 × 10⁻⁷ m), given that the speed of light in a vacuum is 3 × 10⁸ m·s⁻¹.
items.answer: f = 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz

items.prompt: Gamma rays are used in medicine to destroy cancerous cells, but exposure must be very carefully controlled since gamma rays can also damage healthy tissue. Explain, in terms of frequency and energy, why gamma rays are able to penetrate and damage living cells so effectively.
items.answer: Gamma rays have the highest frequency (and shortest wavelength) of all electromagnetic radiation. Within the electromagnetic spectrum, the energy carried by the radiation increases as its frequency increases, so gamma rays carry a very large amount of energy. This high energy allows gamma rays to penetrate deeply into tissue and to damage or destroy the molecules (including DNA) within living cells that they pass through.
items.explanation: This same property — very high energy due to very high frequency — is what makes gamma rays useful for destroying cancerous cells in controlled doses, but also dangerous to healthy cells if exposure is not carefully limited.

items.prompt: A learner argues that infrared radiation must be more harmful than ultraviolet, "because infrared is heat radiation and heat burns you". Evaluate this claim.
items.answer: The claim is wrong. Ultraviolet is far more harmful, because its photons carry enough energy to break chemical bonds.
items.explanation: Infrared is absorbed by molecules and increases their vibration, which we detect as warmth — so the learner is right that it heats, and a strong enough source will burn skin thermally. But the warning of pain arrives first and the damage is superficial and immediate. Ultraviolet photons have a higher frequency and so, from E = hf, more energy each: enough to break bonds in DNA, causing mutations that lead to skin cancer years later. UV produces no sensation of heat at all, which is why sunburn happens without warning and why a cold, bright day can burn more than a hot, hazy one. The learner has ranked the two by the sensation they produce, and the ranking that matters is by energy per photon — on which infrared sits below visible light and ultraviolet above it.

items.prompt: Define a vector quantity.
items.answer: A vector quantity is a physical quantity that has both magnitude and direction.
items.explanation: Examples of vector quantities include force, displacement, velocity and acceleration, each of which requires a direction to be fully specified, unlike a scalar quantity.

items.prompt: Distinguish between a vector quantity and a scalar quantity, giving ONE example of each.
items.answer: A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction (e.g. force), while a scalar quantity has only magnitude, with no associated direction (e.g. mass).
items.explanation: Because a scalar has no direction, scalars are added using ordinary arithmetic, while vectors must be added taking their direction into account (using vector addition methods).

items.prompt: A force of 50 N acts at 30° above the horizontal. A second force of 12 N acts horizontally, in the direction opposite to the horizontal component of the first force. Calculate the horizontal (Fx) and vertical (Fy) components of the 50 N force, and hence the magnitude of the resultant of the two forces.
items.answer: Fx = 50 cos 30° = 43.3 N and Fy = 50 sin 30° = 25 N. The 12 N force is horizontal and opposes Fx, so the resultant horizontal component is 43.3 − 12 = 31.3 N, while the vertical component is unchanged at 25 N. R = √((31.3)² + (25)²) = 40.06 N, at 38.6° above the horizontal.
items.explanation: Forces can only be added along the same line, which is the whole reason for resolving the first one into components. The second force is horizontal, so it changes Fx and leaves Fy completely alone — adding it to the 50 N directly, before resolving, is the mistake this question is built to catch. Once the two perpendicular components of the resultant are known, Pythagoras recombines them into a single magnitude.

items.context: R = √(Fx² + Fy²); tan θ = Fy ÷ Fx
items.prompt: Two forces act on an object: 60 N due east and 80 N due north. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the resultant force.
items.answer: R = 100 N, directed at 53.13° north of east (measured from the 60 N force).
items.explanation: Since the two forces are perpendicular, R = √(60² + 80²) = √(3600 + 6400) = √10000 = 100 N. Direction: θ = tan⁻¹(80 ÷ 60) ≈ 53.13° north of east.

items.context: An object is in equilibrium under three coplanar forces: 40 N due east, 30 N due north, and a third unknown force F₃.
items.prompt: Calculate the magnitude and direction of the third force, F₃, required to keep the object in equilibrium.
items.answer: F₃ = 50 N, directed at 36.87° south of west (i.e. exactly opposite to the resultant of the first two forces).
items.explanation: The resultant of the 40 N (east) and 30 N (north) forces has magnitude √(40² + 30²) = √2500 = 50 N, directed at tan⁻¹(30 ÷ 40) ≈ 36.87° north of east. For the object to be in equilibrium, the net force must be zero, so F₃ (the equilibrant) must be equal in magnitude and exactly opposite in direction to this resultant: 50 N at 36.87° south of west.

items.prompt: State Newton's First Law of Motion.
items.answer: An object continues in a state of rest, or motion at constant velocity in a straight line, unless a net (resultant) force acts on it.
items.explanation: This law is also known as the law of inertia, since it describes an object’s natural tendency to resist any change in its state of motion.

items.prompt: State Newton's Third Law of Motion.
items.answer: When object A exerts a force on object B, object B simultaneously exerts a force of equal magnitude, but in the opposite direction, on object A.
items.explanation: These two forces (often called an "action-reaction pair") always act on two different objects, and always exist simultaneously — neither force can exist without the other.

items.context: Fnet = ma
items.prompt: A net force acts on an 8 kg object, giving it an acceleration of 2.5 m·s⁻². Calculate the magnitude of the net force.
items.answer: Fnet = 20 N

items.context: Component of weight parallel to a frictionless incline: F∥ = mg sin θ
items.prompt: A 5 kg block rests on a frictionless incline of 25°. Calculate the component of the block’s weight acting parallel to the incline surface.
items.explanation: F∥ = mg sin θ = 5 × 9.8 × sin 25° ≈ 20.71 N, directed down the slope.

items.context: A 2 kg trolley on a frictionless horizontal table is connected by a light, inextensible string over a frictionless pulley to a hanging 3 kg mass. a = m₂g ÷ (m₁ + m₂); T = m₁a
items.prompt: Calculate (a) the acceleration of the system, and (b) the tension in the string.

items.context: F∥ = mg sin θ; N = mg cos θ; Ffriction = μN; Fnet = F∥ − Ffriction
items.prompt: A 10 kg block slides down an incline of 30°, where the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.2. Calculate the block’s acceleration down the incline.
Use Newton’s Third Law to explain how a rocket is able to accelerate forward in the vacuum of space, where there is no air for its exhaust gases to "push against".
items.answer: The rocket engine exerts a force on the exhaust gases, expelling them backward at high speed. By Newton’s Third Law, the exhaust gases simultaneously exert an equal and opposite force on the rocket itself, pushing it forward. Since this action-reaction pair exists between the rocket and its own expelled gases (not between the rocket and the surrounding air), the rocket can accelerate forward even in a vacuum, where there is no air or other external medium to push against.
items.explanation: This is a common misconception addressed directly by Newton’s Third Law: rocket propulsion does not rely on exhaust gases pushing against the air, but on the mutual action-reaction force pair between the rocket and the gases it expels, which works equally well (or even better) in a vacuum.

items.prompt: Define refraction.
items.answer: Refraction is the bending of a wave (such as light) as it passes from one medium into another medium of a different optical density, caused by a change in the wave’s speed.
items.explanation: Refraction occurs at the boundary between two media whenever a wave changes speed while crossing that boundary at an angle other than directly perpendicular to it.

items.prompt: State Snell's Law.
items.answer: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, where n₁ and n₂ are the refractive indices of the first and second medium, and θ₁ and θ₂ are the angles of incidence and refraction, both measured from the normal.
items.explanation: Snell’s Law relates the angle at which light enters a new medium to the angle at which it is refracted, based on the refractive indices of the two media involved.

items.context: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂; n(air) = 1.00
items.prompt: A ray of light travels from air (n = 1.00) into glass (n = 1.50), striking the surface at an angle of incidence of 40°. Calculate the angle of refraction.

items.context: sin θc = n₂ ÷ n₁ (light travelling from a denser medium n₁ into a less dense medium n₂)
items.prompt: Calculate the critical angle for light travelling from glass (n = 1.50) into air (n = 1.00).
State the TWO conditions that must both be satisfied for total internal reflection to occur.
items.answer: (1) The light must be travelling from an optically denser medium into an optically less dense medium (from a medium of higher refractive index into one of lower refractive index). (2) The angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle for that pair of media.
items.explanation: If either condition is not met — for example, if the light is travelling into a denser medium, or if the angle of incidence is smaller than the critical angle — the light will simply refract (and partially reflect) at the boundary, rather than undergoing total internal reflection.

items.prompt: A cable supplier recommends the thickest available optical fibre for a long data link, on the grounds that "a wider core lets in more light, so the signal will be stronger and clearer". Evaluate the supplier's reasoning.
items.answer: Stronger, probably. Clearer, no — a wide core is the cause of the blurring that limits a long link.
items.explanation: A wider core does accept light over a larger range of angles, so more of it enters. That is also the problem. Rays entering at different angles travel by different numbers of reflections and therefore along paths of different lengths: a ray going almost straight down the axis arrives before one zig-zagging steeply, even though both travel at the same speed. A pulse sent in as a sharp spike emerges spread out, and on a long link consecutive pulses overlap until the receiver can no longer tell them apart. This is modal dispersion, and it is why long-distance links use SINGLE-MODE fibre with a core only about 9 µm across — narrow enough that essentially one path exists. The supplier has correctly identified how to collect more light and has chosen the design that destroys the timing, and on a data link it is the timing that carries the information.

items.prompt: Define a wavefront.
items.answer: A wavefront is an imaginary line (in two dimensions) or surface (in three dimensions) joining all points of a wave that are in phase with each other.
items.explanation: A line drawn perpendicular to a set of wavefronts indicates the direction in which the wave is travelling (the ray direction).

items.prompt: State Huygens' principle.
items.answer: Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary (new) wavelets, and the new wavefront at a later time is found by drawing a surface tangent to all of these secondary wavelets.
items.explanation: Huygens’ principle provides a geometric method for constructing how a wavefront will propagate over time, and is used to explain phenomena such as diffraction.

items.prompt: Describe how the amount of diffraction of a wave passing through a narrow slit changes as the width of the slit is decreased (with wavelength kept constant).
items.answer: As the slit width decreases (becoming closer to the size of the wavelength), the amount of diffraction (the spreading of the wave into the region behind the slit) increases.
items.explanation: Diffraction is most pronounced when the size of the gap (or obstacle) is comparable to or smaller than the wavelength of the wave, which is why narrowing a slit increases the observed spreading of the wave passing through it.

items.prompt: Explain why radio waves diffract noticeably around large obstacles such as buildings and hills, while visible light passing the same obstacles shows no noticeable diffraction.
items.answer: Radio waves have a much longer wavelength than visible light — often comparable in size to large obstacles such as buildings and hills — so they diffract (spread) noticeably around such obstacles. Visible light has a very short wavelength (a tiny fraction of a millimetre), which is minuscule compared to the size of everyday obstacles such as buildings; since noticeable diffraction requires the obstacle (or gap) size to be comparable to the wavelength, visible light shows no observable diffraction around such large objects, and instead simply forms a sharp shadow.
items.explanation: This is a direct consequence of the general diffraction principle: the amount of diffraction observed depends on the size of the wavelength relative to the size of the obstacle or gap, not on the wave type itself.

items.prompt: Using Huygens’ principle, explain why a wavefront passing through a narrow slit emerges on the far side as a curved (circular or semi-circular), spreading wavefront, rather than continuing as a straight wavefront.
items.answer: According to Huygens’ principle, every point along the original wavefront (including the small section of it passing through the narrow slit) acts as a source of new, secondary wavelets, spreading out in all directions from that point. When the slit is narrow enough, only a very small section of the original wavefront passes through it, so essentially only a single point (or a very small number of points) acts as a secondary source on the far side, producing wavelets that spread out in a circular (or semi-circular) pattern in every direction, rather than continuing to reinforce a flat, straight wavefront (which would require many adjacent points, spread across a wide front, all contributing wavelets that combine to maintain a flat shape).
items.explanation: This is precisely why diffraction becomes more pronounced as a slit becomes narrower: a very narrow slit isolates such a small section of the original wavefront that it behaves almost like a single point source of new circular wavelets, producing very noticeable spreading, whereas a wide slit still contains many adjacent points whose combined secondary wavelets largely preserve the original straight wavefront shape.

items.prompt: State the principle of conservation of charge.
items.answer: Charge cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one object (or location) to another; the total charge of an isolated system remains constant.
items.explanation: This principle underlies processes such as charging by friction or by contact, in which charge moves between objects but the total amount of charge in the isolated system is unchanged.

items.prompt: State Coulomb's Law.
items.answer: The electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the two charges, and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
items.explanation: This is expressed mathematically as F = kQ₁Q₂ ÷ r², where k is the Coulomb constant (9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻²).

items.prompt: Two point charges, +3 μC and +4 μC, are placed 0.2 m apart. The +3 μC charge is carried by a small sphere of mass 7.5 g that is free to move; the other charge is held fixed. Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between the charges, and hence the magnitude of the initial acceleration of the sphere. (k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²·C⁻²)
items.answer: F = kQ₁Q₂/r² = (9.0 × 10⁹)(3 × 10⁻⁶)(4 × 10⁻⁶) ÷ (0.2)² = 2.7 N. Both charges are positive, so the force is a repulsion and the sphere accelerates away from the fixed charge. Converting the mass, 7.5 g = 7.50 × 10⁻³ kg, a = F/m = 2.7 ÷ 7.50 × 10⁻³ = 360 m·s⁻².
items.explanation: The two halves belong to different topics and the second cannot start until the first has finished: Coulomb’s law gives the force, and only then does Newton’s second law turn that force into an acceleration. Two conversions decide whether the answer is right — microcoulombs to coulombs and grams to kilograms — and getting either wrong still produces a plausible-looking number. Note the acceleration is only the INITIAL one: as the sphere moves away, r grows, the force falls off as 1/r², and the acceleration drops with it, so this value holds at the instant of release and not afterwards.

items.context: E = kQ ÷ r²
items.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the electric field at a point 0.3 m from a point charge of +6 μC.

items.context: Three point charges lie on a straight line: Q₁ = +4 μC, Q₂ = +2 μC (0.2 m from Q₁), and Q₃ = −3 μC (0.3 m from Q₂, on the far side from Q₁).
items.prompt: Calculate the magnitude and direction of the net force on Q₂ due to Q₁ and Q₃.
items.answer: Fnet ≈ 2.40 N, directed away from Q₁ (toward Q₃).
items.explanation: Force from Q₁ on Q₂ (repulsive, since both positive): F₁₂ = kQ₁Q₂ ÷ r₁₂² = (9.0×10⁹ × 4×10⁻⁶ × 2×10⁻⁶) ÷ (0.2)² = 1.80 N, pushing Q₂ away from Q₁. Force from Q₃ on Q₂ (attractive, since opposite signs): F₂₃ = kQ₂Q₃ ÷ r₂₃² = (9.0×10⁹ × 2×10⁻⁶ × 3×10⁻⁶) ÷ (0.3)² = 0.60 N, pulling Q₂ toward Q₃ (i.e. also away from Q₁, in the same direction). Since both forces act in the same direction, Fnet = F₁₂ + F₂₃ = 1.80 + 0.60 = 2.40 N, directed away from Q₁.

items.prompt: A charged object carries a charge of −1.6 μC. Calculate the number of excess electrons responsible for this charge, and then calculate the object’s new charge if 4.00 × 10¹² of those excess electrons are removed. (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
items.answer: n = Q/e = (1.6 × 10⁻⁶) ÷ (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 1.00 × 10¹³ excess electrons. Removing 4.00 × 10¹² of them leaves 6.00 × 10¹² excess electrons, so the new charge is 6.00 × 10¹² × (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 9.60 × 10⁻⁷ C, or −0.96 μC.
items.explanation: Charge is quantised, which is what makes the first step possible at all: every charge is a whole number of elementary charges, so dividing by e counts them. The second step is where the reasoning sits — removing ELECTRONS makes an object LESS negative, not more, because it is the surplus of electrons that carries the negative sign. The object stays negative here only because electrons remain in surplus; remove enough of them and the charge would pass through zero and become positive.

items.prompt: State the right-hand rule used to determine the direction of the magnetic field around a straight, current-carrying conductor.
items.answer: If the thumb of the right hand points in the direction of conventional current flow, the curled fingers indicate the direction of the circular magnetic field lines around the conductor.
items.explanation: This rule allows the direction of the (otherwise invisible) magnetic field around a conductor to be determined directly from the known direction of current flow.

items.prompt: Describe the shape of the magnetic field lines around a long, straight, current-carrying conductor.
items.answer: The magnetic field lines form concentric circles around the conductor, in a plane perpendicular to the conductor.
items.explanation: The magnetic field is strongest closest to the conductor and becomes weaker (the circles become more widely spaced) further from the conductor.

items.prompt: Describe the magnetic field pattern produced by a solenoid (a coil of current-carrying wire), and compare it to the field of a bar magnet.
items.answer: A solenoid produces a magnetic field pattern very similar to that of a bar magnet: field lines emerge from one end (behaving like a north pole), curve around the outside of the solenoid, and re-enter at the other end (behaving like a south pole), with a strong, roughly uniform field running along the inside of the solenoid.
items.explanation: This similarity arises because a solenoid is essentially many individual current loops stacked together, and their combined magnetic fields reinforce each other along the axis of the coil, producing an overall field pattern that closely resembles that of a simple bar magnet.

items.prompt: State THREE factors that increase the strength of the magnetic field produced by a solenoid.
items.answer: (1) Increasing the current flowing through the solenoid. (2) Increasing the number of turns of wire in the solenoid. (3) Inserting a soft-iron core inside the solenoid.
items.explanation: Each of these factors increases the total magnetic effect produced: more current means a stronger field per turn, more turns means more individual current loops contributing to the overall field, and a soft-iron core becomes magnetised itself and significantly strengthens the resulting field.

items.prompt: Explain why a current-carrying conductor placed in an external magnetic field experiences a force (the motor effect), and describe how the direction of this force can be determined.
items.answer: A current-carrying conductor has moving charges within it, and moving charges in a magnetic field experience a magnetic force. Because the conductor as a whole carries current through the external magnetic field, the combined force on all these moving charges results in a net force on the conductor itself. The direction of this force can be determined using the right-hand rule for the motor effect: if the fingers of the right hand point in the direction of the external magnetic field, and the thumb points in the direction of conventional current flow, the palm pushes in the direction of the resulting force on the conductor (alternatively stated using the right-hand slap/palm rule, depending on the specific convention taught).
items.explanation: This force is the basis of the electric motor: by placing a current-carrying coil within an external magnetic field, the resulting force on the coil (whose direction reverses appropriately as the coil rotates, if using a split-ring commutator) causes the coil to rotate continuously.

items.prompt: State Ohm's Law.
items.answer: The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature (and other physical conditions) of the conductor remain constant.
items.explanation: This relationship is expressed as V = IR, where R (resistance) remains constant for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature.

items.context: V = IR; series: Rtotal = R₁ + R₂
items.prompt: A 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor are connected in series to a 12 V battery. Calculate (a) the total resistance of the circuit, and (b) the current supplied by the battery.
items.answer: (a) Rtotal = 12 Ω  (b) I = 1.0 A
items.explanation: (a) Rtotal = R₁ + R₂ = 4 + 8 = 12 Ω. (b) I = V ÷ Rtotal = 12 ÷ 12 = 1.0 A.

items.context: 1/Rp = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂
items.prompt: A 6 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Calculate the equivalent resistance of the combination.
items.answer: Rp = 4.0 Ω

items.context: A 4 Ω resistor is connected in series with a parallel combination of a 6 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor.
items.prompt: Calculate the total resistance of this combined series-parallel circuit.
items.answer: Rtotal = 8.0 Ω
items.explanation: First find the parallel combination: 1/Rp = 1/6 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4, so Rp = 4.0 Ω. Then add this in series with the 4 Ω resistor: Rtotal = 4 + 4 = 8.0 Ω.

items.prompt: A learner measures 12 V across a battery's terminals with nothing connected, then 10.5 V while it drives a circuit, and concludes the battery is faulty and losing charge rapidly. Evaluate this conclusion.
items.answer: The conclusion is wrong. A terminal voltage that drops under load is normal, and the size of the drop measures the internal resistance.
items.explanation: Every real cell has internal resistance r, from the chemistry and conducting paths inside it. With nothing connected, no current flows, so nothing is lost inside and the voltmeter reads the full emf: ε = 12 V. Once current I flows, the charge must pass through r as well, dropping Ir inside the cell, so what reaches the terminals is Vterm = ε − Ir = 10.5 V. The 1.5 V difference is the lost volts, and if the current were known, r = 1.5 ÷ I could be worked out from it. A genuinely failing battery shows itself differently — its INTERNAL RESISTANCE has risen, so the same load pulls the terminal voltage down much further than it used to. The learner has observed the standard behaviour of a working cell and read it as a fault.

items.prompt: The gravitational force between two objects is F. The mass of EACH object is doubled and the distance between their centres is halved. The gravitational force is now …
items.explanation: F = Gm₁m₂/r². Doubling both masses multiplies F by 2 × 2 = 4; halving r multiplies F by 2² = 4. Altogether F is multiplied by 16.

items.prompt: A book rests on a table. According to Newton’s Third Law, the reaction to the gravitational force of the Earth on the book is the …

options.label: normal force of the table on the book.
gravitational force of the book on the Earth.
force of the book on the table.

items.answer: gravitational force of the book on the Earth.
items.explanation: An action-reaction pair acts on two different objects and is of the same type. The Earth pulls the book, so the book pulls the Earth. The normal force is equal and opposite to the weight, but it is not the reaction to it.

items.prompt: From the same height and at the same instant, ball P is DROPPED and ball Q is THROWN vertically downwards. Ignoring air resistance, which ONE of the following is correct while they fall?

options.label: Q has a greater acceleration than P.
P and Q have the same acceleration.
P and Q have the same velocity.
P and Q reach the ground at the same time.

items.answer: P and Q have the same acceleration.
items.explanation: Both balls are projectiles, so each accelerates at g downwards. Q starts with a greater velocity, so it keeps a greater velocity and lands first.

items.prompt: The area under a graph of NET FORCE against TIME for an object is equal to the …

options.label: change in momentum of the object.
change in kinetic energy of the object.

items.answer: change in momentum of the object.
items.explanation: The area is FnetΔt, which is the impulse, and the impulse equals the change in momentum.

items.prompt: A box slides along a rough HORIZONTAL floor. The work done on the box by the NORMAL force is …

options.label: equal to the work done by friction.

items.answer: zero.
items.explanation: W = FΔx cos θ. The normal force is perpendicular to the displacement, so θ = 90° and cos 90° = 0.

items.prompt: Doctors use the Doppler effect with ultrasound to measure the …

options.label: rate of blood flow in an artery.

items.answer: rate of blood flow in an artery.
items.explanation: Ultrasound reflected from moving blood cells changes frequency. The size of the change gives the speed of the blood.

items.prompt: Two point charges exert an electrostatic force F on each other. The charge on ONE of them is doubled and the distance between them is also doubled. The force is now …
items.answer: ½F
items.explanation: F = kQ₁Q₂/r². Doubling one charge doubles F; doubling r divides F by 4. 2 ÷ 4 = ½.

items.prompt: Three identical bulbs are connected in PARALLEL to a battery with NEGLIGIBLE internal resistance. One bulb blows. What happens to the brightness of the other two bulbs?
items.answer: They stay the same.
items.explanation: With no internal resistance, the potential difference across each parallel branch stays equal to the emf, so the current in each remaining bulb, and its power, does not change.

items.prompt: The rms value of an alternating potential difference is the …

options.label: largest value that the potential difference reaches.
average value of the potential difference over one cycle.
DC potential difference that dissipates the same amount of energy in a resistor.

items.answer: DC potential difference that dissipates the same amount of energy in a resistor.
items.explanation: That is the definition of the rms value. For a sine wave it is the peak value divided by √2; the average over a full cycle is zero.

items.prompt: Which ONE of the following colours of light has photons with the GREATEST energy?
items.answer: Violet
items.explanation: E = hf. Violet light has the highest frequency (shortest wavelength) of the four, so its photons have the most energy.

sections.title: A lawnmower pushed across a lawn

items.context: A gardener pushes a 12 kg lawnmower across a flat, horizontal lawn. The gardener pushes along the handle with a force of 80 N directed at 40° BELOW the horizontal, and the lawnmower moves at CONSTANT VELOCITY. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
items.prompt: Define the term normal force.
items.answer: The force exerted by a surface on an object in contact with it, acting perpendicular to the surface.
items.explanation: The normal force is always at 90° to the surface. It is not always equal to the weight -- here it is larger.

items.context: A gardener pushes a 12 kg lawnmower across a flat, horizontal lawn. The gardener pushes along the handle with a force of 80 N directed at 40° BELOW the horizontal, and the lawnmower moves at CONSTANT VELOCITY. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
items.prompt: Draw a labelled free-body diagram showing ALL the forces acting on the lawnmower. (Describe your diagram in words: name each force and give its direction.)
items.answer: Four forces: weight (w or Fg) vertically downwards; normal force (N) vertically upwards; the applied force (F) along the handle, 40° below the horizontal, in the direction of motion; kinetic friction (fk) horizontal, opposite to the motion.
items.explanation: One mark for each correctly labelled force with the correct direction. The applied force points forwards and downwards, because the gardener pushes along the handle.

items.context: A gardener pushes a 12 kg lawnmower across a flat, horizontal lawn. The gardener pushes along the handle with a force of 80 N directed at 40° BELOW the horizontal, and the lawnmower moves at CONSTANT VELOCITY. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
items.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the normal force acting on the lawnmower.
items.explanation: There is no vertical acceleration, so the upward force balances the downward forces: N = mg + F sin 40° = 12(9,8) + 80 sin 40° = 117,6 + 51,42 = 169,02 N.

items.context:
A gardener pushes a 12 kg lawnmower across a flat, horizontal lawn. The gardener pushes along the handle with a force of 80 N directed at 40° BELOW the horizontal, and the lawnmower moves at CONSTANT VELOCITY. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
The normal force on the lawnmower is 169,02 N.
items.prompt: Calculate the coefficient of kinetic friction between the lawnmower and the lawn.
items.explanation: Constant velocity, so the net horizontal force is zero: fk = F cos 40° = 80 cos 40° = 61,28 N. μk = fk ÷ N = 61,28 ÷ 169,02 = 0,36.

items.context: A gardener pushes a 12 kg lawnmower across a flat, horizontal lawn. The gardener pushes along the handle with a force of 80 N directed at 40° BELOW the horizontal, and the lawnmower moves at CONSTANT VELOCITY. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
items.prompt: The gardener now PULLS the lawnmower backwards with a force of 80 N directed at 40° ABOVE the horizontal. How will the kinetic frictional force on the lawnmower compare with its value in QUESTION 2.4? Choose from INCREASES, DECREASES or REMAINS THE SAME. Explain.
items.answer: DECREASES. The vertical component of the force now acts upwards, so the normal force decreases (N = mg − F sin 40° = 66,18 N instead of 169,02 N). Since fk = μkN and μk is unchanged, the frictional force decreases.
items.explanation: The coefficient of friction depends only on the two surfaces. What changes is how hard the lawnmower presses on the lawn, which is why pulling a mower is easier than pushing it.

items.context: A firework shell is fired vertically upwards from the ground and reaches a maximum height of 45 m above the ground. Ignore air resistance, and ignore the height of the launch tube. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
items.prompt: What is meant by free fall?
items.answer: Motion during which the only force acting on the object is the gravitational force.
items.explanation: A shell in free fall accelerates at g downwards on the way up, at the top and on the way down.

items.context: A firework shell is fired vertically upwards from the ground and reaches a maximum height of 45 m above the ground. Ignore air resistance, and ignore the height of the launch tube. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
items.prompt: Calculate the speed at which the shell is fired.
items.explanation: At the maximum height vf = 0. Taking upwards as positive: vf² = vi² + 2aΔy, so 0 = vi² + 2(−9,8)(45), vi² = 882 and vi = 29,70 m·s⁻¹.

items.context:
A firework shell is fired vertically upwards from the ground and reaches a maximum height of 45 m above the ground. Ignore air resistance, and ignore the height of the launch tube. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
The shell is fired at 29,70 m·s⁻¹.
items.prompt: Assume the shell does not explode. Calculate the total time from when it is fired until it lands back at the launch point.
items.explanation: Time to the top: vf = vi + aΔt, so 0 = 29,70 − 9,8Δt and Δt = 3,03 s. The motion is symmetrical, so the time back down is the same: 2 × 3,03 = 6,06 s.

items.context:
A firework shell is fired vertically upwards from the ground and reaches a maximum height of 45 m above the ground. Ignore air resistance, and ignore the height of the launch tube. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
The shell is fired at 29,70 m·s⁻¹. Assume it does not explode.
items.prompt: Calculate the TWO times at which the shell is 20 m above the ground.
items.answer: 0,77 s (on the way up) and 5,29 s (on the way down)
items.explanation: Taking upwards as positive: Δy = viΔt + ½aΔt², so 20 = 29,70Δt − 4,9Δt². Rearranged: 4,9Δt² − 29,70Δt + 20 = 0. Δt = [29,70 ± √(29,70² − 4(4,9)(20))] ÷ 9,8 = (29,70 ± 22,14) ÷ 9,8, giving 0,77 s and 5,29 s.

items.context:
A firework shell is fired vertically upwards from the ground and reaches a maximum height of 45 m above the ground. Ignore air resistance, and ignore the height of the launch tube. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
Assume the shell does not explode. It reaches 45 m after 3,03 s and lands after 6,06 s.
items.prompt: Sketch a POSITION versus time graph for the shell, from when it is fired until it lands. Use the ground as the zero position and take upwards as positive. Describe the graph in words, giving its shape and the values at the key points.
items.answer: A curve (half a parabola each side of the top, opening downwards) starting at 0 m at t = 0, rising to a maximum of 45 m at t = 3,03 s, and returning to 0 m at t = 6,06 s.
items.explanation: The velocity changes at a constant rate, so position against time is a parabola. Its gradient is steep at the start and end and zero at the top. Marks: shape, starting point, maximum and landing time.

items.context: On a frictionless horizontal track, trolley A of mass 2 kg moves east at 3 m·s⁻¹ and trolley B of mass 1 kg moves west at 2 m·s⁻¹. They collide head-on. Immediately after the collision, trolley A moves east at 0,5 m·s⁻¹.
items.prompt: State the principle of conservation of linear momentum in words.
items.answer: The total linear momentum of an isolated system remains constant (is conserved).
items.explanation: An isolated system is one on which the net external force is zero. The track is frictionless, so the two trolleys form one.

items.context: On a frictionless horizontal track, trolley A of mass 2 kg moves east at 3 m·s⁻¹ and trolley B of mass 1 kg moves west at 2 m·s⁻¹. They collide head-on. Immediately after the collision, trolley A moves east at 0,5 m·s⁻¹.
items.prompt: Calculate the velocity of trolley B immediately after the collision.
items.answer: 3 m·s⁻¹ east
items.explanation: Taking east as positive: Σpbefore = Σpafter. 2(3) + 1(−2) = 2(0,5) + 1(vB), so 4 = 1 + vB and vB = 3 m·s⁻¹ east.

items.context:
On a frictionless horizontal track, trolley A of mass 2 kg moves east at 3 m·s⁻¹ and trolley B of mass 1 kg moves west at 2 m·s⁻¹. They collide head-on. Immediately after the collision, trolley A moves east at 0,5 m·s⁻¹.
After the collision, trolley B moves east at 3 m·s⁻¹.
items.prompt: Is the collision ELASTIC or INELASTIC? Show a calculation to support your answer.
items.answer: INELASTIC. Total Ek before = 11 J; total Ek after = 4,75 J.
items.explanation: Ek before = ½(2)(3²) + ½(1)(2²) = 9 + 2 = 11 J. Ek after = ½(2)(0,5²) + ½(1)(3²) = 0,25 + 4,5 = 4,75 J. Kinetic energy is not conserved, so the collision is inelastic.

items.context:
On a frictionless horizontal track, trolley A of mass 2 kg moves east at 3 m·s⁻¹ and trolley B of mass 1 kg moves west at 2 m·s⁻¹. They collide head-on. Immediately after the collision, trolley A moves east at 0,5 m·s⁻¹.
After the collision, trolley B moves east at 3 m·s⁻¹. The trolleys are in contact for 0,05 s.
items.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the average force that trolley A exerts on trolley B during the collision.
items.explanation: Taking east as positive: FnetΔt = m(vf − vi) = 1(3 − (−2)) = 5 N·s. F = 5 ÷ 0,05 = 100 N (east). B reverses direction, so the change in velocity is 5 m·s⁻¹, not 1 m·s⁻¹.

items.context: A 2 kg block is released from rest at the top of a curved ramp, 1,2 m above a horizontal floor. The ramp is frictionless. At the bottom of the ramp the block slides onto a rough horizontal floor and comes to rest after sliding 3 m along it. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
items.prompt: Define the term non-conservative force.
items.answer: A force for which the work done in moving an object between two points depends on the path taken.
items.explanation: Friction is non-conservative: the longer the path, the more work it does against the motion.

items.context: A 2 kg block is released from rest at the top of a curved ramp, 1,2 m above a horizontal floor. The ramp is frictionless. At the bottom of the ramp the block slides onto a rough horizontal floor and comes to rest after sliding 3 m along it. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
items.prompt: Use the principle of conservation of mechanical energy to calculate the speed of the block at the bottom of the ramp.
items.explanation: The ramp is frictionless, so (Ep + Ek)top = (Ep + Ek)bottom: 2(9,8)(1,2) + 0 = 0 + ½(2)v². 23,52 = v², so v = 4,85 m·s⁻¹.

items.context: A 2 kg block is released from rest at the top of a curved ramp, 1,2 m above a horizontal floor. The ramp is frictionless. At the bottom of the ramp the block slides onto a rough horizontal floor and comes to rest after sliding 3 m along it. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
items.prompt: Draw a labelled free-body diagram of the block while it slides along the rough horizontal floor. (Describe it in words.)
items.answer: Three forces: weight (w) vertically downwards; normal force (N) vertically upwards; kinetic friction (fk) horizontal, opposite to the direction of motion.
items.explanation: No force pushes the block forwards once it leaves the ramp: it keeps moving only because of its kinetic energy. One mark per force.

items.context:
A 2 kg block is released from rest at the top of a curved ramp, 1,2 m above a horizontal floor. The ramp is frictionless. At the bottom of the ramp the block slides onto a rough horizontal floor and comes to rest after sliding 3 m along it. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
The block reaches the bottom of the ramp at 4,85 m·s⁻¹.
items.prompt: Use the work-energy theorem to calculate the magnitude of the frictional force on the block on the horizontal floor.
items.explanation: Only friction does work along the floor: Wnet = ΔEk, so f(3)cos 180° = 0 − ½(2)(4,85²). −3f = −23,52, so f = 7,84 N.

items.context: A 2 kg block is released from rest at the top of a curved ramp, 1,2 m above a horizontal floor. The ramp is frictionless. At the bottom of the ramp the block slides onto a rough horizontal floor and comes to rest after sliding 3 m along it. Take g = 9,8 m·s⁻².
items.prompt: The block is replaced by a 4 kg block made of the same material and released from the same height. How will the distance it slides along the floor compare with 3 m? Choose from GREATER THAN, LESS THAN or EQUAL TO. Explain.
items.answer: EQUAL TO. Doubling the mass doubles the kinetic energy at the bottom, but it also doubles the normal force and so the frictional force (f = μkmg). The stopping distance mgh ÷ μkmg = h ÷ μk does not depend on the mass.
items.explanation: The mass cancels out, just as it does for a projectile. Only the height and the surfaces matter.

items.context: A drone carries a buzzer that emits sound at a frequency of 2 000 Hz. The drone flies in a straight line directly AWAY from a stationary learner at constant velocity. The learner detects a frequency of 1 900 Hz. Take the speed of sound in air as 340 m·s⁻¹.
items.prompt: State the Doppler effect.
items.answer: The change in frequency (or pitch) of the sound detected by a listener because the sound source and the listener have different velocities relative to the medium of sound propagation.
items.explanation: Here the source (the drone) moves and the listener is still.

items.context: A drone carries a buzzer that emits sound at a frequency of 2 000 Hz. The drone flies in a straight line directly AWAY from a stationary learner at constant velocity. The learner detects a frequency of 1 900 Hz. Take the speed of sound in air as 340 m·s⁻¹.
items.prompt: Calculate the speed of the drone.

items.context: A drone carries a buzzer that emits sound at a frequency of 2 000 Hz. The drone flies in a straight line directly AWAY from a stationary learner at constant velocity. The learner detects a frequency of 1 900 Hz. Take the speed of sound in air as 340 m·s⁻¹.
items.prompt: Calculate the wavelength of the sound that the learner detects.
items.explanation: v = fλ, so λ = 340 ÷ 1 900 = 0,179 m. Behind a receding source the wavefronts are spread out, so this is longer than the emitted wavelength (340 ÷ 2 000 = 0,17 m).

questions.context: Two charges lie on the x-axis: QA = +5 μC at x = 0 and QB = −3 μC at x = 0,40 m. A small positive test charge is placed at x = 0,20 m, midway between them. k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².

questions.answer: From QA: E = kQ/r² = (9 × 10⁹)(5 × 10⁻⁶) ÷ (0,20)² = 0,045 ÷ 0,04 = 1,125 × 10⁶ N/C, directed away from QA because QA is positive, so to the right. From QB: E = (9 × 10⁹)(3 × 10⁻⁶) ÷ (0,20)² = 0,027 ÷ 0,04 = 0,675 × 10⁶ N/C, directed towards QB because QB is negative, so also to the right. Both point right, so the net field is 1,125 × 10⁶ + 0,675 × 10⁶ = 1,80 × 10⁶ N/C to the right. They add because the charges have OPPOSITE signs: the field of a positive charge points away from it and the field of a negative charge points towards it, so at a point between them both arrows point the same way -- from the positive towards the negative.
questions.explanation: Work in one dimension by treating right as positive and left as negative, then add. The reasoning worth keeping is the sign rule: between two LIKE charges the fields oppose and can cancel, between two UNLIKE charges they reinforce and can never cancel anywhere between them. Deciding that before calculating tells you whether a zero-field point is even possible.

questions.context: Two charges are fixed on a straight line: Q1 = +9 μC at x = 0 and Q2 = +4 μC at x = 0,50 m.
questions.prompt: Explain why a point of zero net electric field must lie BETWEEN these two charges rather than outside them, and state whether it lies closer to Q1 or to Q2. Give a reason.
questions.answer: Both charges are positive, so each produces a field pointing away from itself. At any point between them the two fields point in opposite directions -- away from Q1 is to the right, away from Q2 is to the left -- so they can cancel. At any point outside the pair, both fields point the same way: to the left of Q1 both point left, and to the right of Q2 both point right, so they add and can never sum to zero. The zero point therefore lies between them. It lies closer to Q2, the smaller charge. Field strength falls off with distance, so to balance the larger charge Q1 the point must be further from Q1 and nearer Q2 -- being closer compensates Q2 for being weaker.
questions.explanation: Answer this by reasoning about DIRECTIONS before touching any numbers: cancellation needs two arrows pointing opposite ways, and that only happens between two like charges or outside a pair of unlike ones. The "closer to the smaller charge" conclusion is worth holding as a check on any calculation -- an answer placing the null point nearer the bigger charge is wrong without needing to be re-worked.

questions.prompt: Explain, using the collision theory, why increasing the concentration of an acid increases the rate at which it reacts with magnesium ribbon.

questions.prompt: State THREE features of a reversible reaction that has reached dynamic equilibrium.

questions.prompt: Explain why chemical equilibrium is described as dynamic and not static.

questions.explanation: Equilibrium needs every substance to stay available to react; a closed system keeps them all in.

questions.context: Solution A is 0.1 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid, a strong acid. Solution B is 0.1 mol/dm3 ethanoic acid, a weak acid.
questions.prompt: (a) Calculate the pH of solution A. (b) State whether the pH of solution B is higher or lower than that of solution A, and explain why. (c) Explain why equal volumes of A and B both require the same volume of 0.1 mol/dm3 sodium hydroxide to neutralise them completely.
questions.answer: (a) Hydrochloric acid ionises completely, so [H3O+] = 0.1 = 1 x 10^-1 mol/dm3, and pH = -log(1 x 10^-1) = 1. (b) Solution B has a higher pH. Ethanoic acid is weak, so it ionises only partially and releases far fewer hydronium ions at the same concentration; a lower [H3O+] means a higher pH. (c) Neutralisation depends on the total moles of acid available to react, not on how much has ionised at any moment. Both solutions contain the same number of moles of acid, and as the ionised acid is neutralised the weak acid ionises further until all of it has reacted, so the same volume of base is needed.
questions.explanation: This question separates strength from concentration, which is the distinction most often confused. Part (c) is the decisive one: pH measures how much acid has ionised, while a titration measures how much acid is present in total, so a weak acid and a strong acid of the same concentration behave very differently on a pH meter and identically in a titration.

questions.context: A volume of 25,0 mℓ of hydrochloric acid of unknown concentration is titrated with sodium hydroxide of concentration 0,100 mol·dm⁻³. The pH of the mixture is recorded as the base is added, giving the curve shown.
questions.prompt: Read off from the graph the volume of sodium hydroxide needed to reach the equivalence point and the pH at that point. Hence calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid.
questions.answer: From the graph, the near-vertical section crosses the middle of its rise at 25 mℓ of sodium hydroxide added, and the pH there is 7. That is the equivalence point. For the concentration: n = cV, so n(NaOH) = 0,100 × 0,0250 = 2,50 × 10⁻³ mol. The balanced equation is HCℓ + NaOH → NaCℓ + H₂O, a mole ratio of 1 : 1, so n(HCℓ) = 2,50 × 10⁻³ mol as well. That was contained in 25,0 mℓ, so c(HCℓ) = n / V = 2,50 × 10⁻³ / 0,0250 = 0,100 mol·dm⁻³.
questions.explanation: Two habits are being drilled here. The first is converting millilitres to cubic decimetres before substituting: 25,0 mℓ is 0,0250 dm³, and forgetting this is the single commonest error in a titration calculation, because the answer that comes out still looks reasonable. The second is reading the equivalence point from the steep section rather than from where the curve flattens — the equivalence point is the midpoint of the vertical rise, not the top of it. The equal concentrations here are a coincidence of the numbers, not a rule; had the ratio been 1 : 2, as with H₂SO₄ and NaOH, the concentrations would differ by a factor of two even with equal volumes.

memo.text: Equivalence point at 25 mℓ of NaOH added
n = cV, with the volume converted to dm³

questions.context: Looking at this curve, a learner writes: "The equivalence point of a titration is always at pH 7, because that is where the acid and the base cancel each other out exactly."
questions.prompt: Evaluate the learner’s claim. State whether it holds in general, and use the titration of ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide to support your answer.
questions.answer: The claim is wrong in general, although it happens to be true for the titration shown. The equivalence point is defined by MOLES, not by pH: it is the point at which exactly enough base has been added to react with all of the acid, in the ratio the balanced equation gives. What the pH is at that point depends on the salt that has been formed. For this curve — hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide, a strong acid with a strong base — the salt is NaCℓ. Neither Na⁺ nor Cℓ⁻ reacts with water to any measurable extent, so the solution at equivalence is neutral and the pH is 7. The learner has generalised from this one case. For ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide, a WEAK acid with a strong base, the salt formed is sodium ethanoate. The ethanoate ion is the conjugate base of a weak acid and it hydrolyses: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻. That reaction releases hydroxide ions, so the solution at the equivalence point is basic and the pH is above 7, typically around 8,7. The mirror case is a weak base with a strong acid, such as ammonia with hydrochloric acid, where the ammonium ion hydrolyses to release hydronium ions and the equivalence point lies below pH 7.
questions.explanation: This matters practically, not just definitionally: the pH at equivalence is what decides which indicator you may use. An indicator must change colour within the steep section of the curve, so phenolphthalein, which turns between about pH 8,3 and 10, is right for a weak acid with a strong base and wrong for a weak base with a strong acid; methyl orange, changing between about pH 3,1 and 4,4, is the other way round. For a strong acid with a strong base the vertical section spans roughly pH 3 to pH 11 and either indicator works — which is another reason this case misleads learners into thinking the choice never matters.

memo.text: The claim is false in general; it holds only for a strong acid with a strong base
The equivalence point is defined by the mole ratio, not by pH
NaCℓ does not hydrolyse, which is why THIS curve is neutral at equivalence
Sodium ethanoate hydrolyses: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻
The released OH⁻ puts the equivalence point above pH 7 for a weak acid with a strong base

questions.context: A 2 kg block is pulled across a rough horizontal surface with a constant horizontal force of 15 N. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface is 0.2. Use g = 9.8 m/s2.
questions.prompt: (a) Calculate the frictional force. (b) Determine the net force acting on the block. (c) Find the acceleration of the block. (d) Explain how the coefficient of friction affects motion in real-life situations, giving one case where a high value is wanted and one where a low value is wanted.
questions.answer: (a) On a horizontal surface with a horizontal applied force, N = m g = 2 x 9.8 = 19.6 N, so f = mu N = 0.2 x 19.6 = 3.92 N opposing the motion. (b) Fnet = 15 - 3.92 = 11.08 N in the direction of the pull. (c) a = Fnet / m = 11.08 / 2 = 5.54 m/s2 in the direction of the pull. (d) The coefficient sets how much friction a surface pair gives for a given normal force. A high value is wanted between tyres and the road, because the friction is what lets a car accelerate, turn and brake; on a wet road mu drops, the available friction falls and the braking distance grows. A low value is wanted between moving machine parts, so oil is used to cut wear and the energy wasted as heat.
questions.explanation: The normal force has to be found before the friction, because f = mu N and not mu m. Part (d) carries as many marks as the calculations and is answered from the same equation: mu is a property of the two surfaces in contact, so changing the surfaces, by wetting the road or oiling a bearing, changes the motion without changing any of the forces applied.

questions.context: A wooden block of mass 4 kg rests, without sliding, on a plank inclined at 25° to the horizontal.
questions.prompt: Draw a labelled free-body diagram showing all the forces acting on the block. Then state which TWO of those forces have components that balance along the slope, and explain how you know the friction is static rather than kinetic.
questions.answer: Three forces act on the block, each drawn as an arrow starting at the block and pointing away from it: the weight w acting vertically downwards; the normal force N acting perpendicular to the surface of the slope, away from it; and friction f acting UP the slope, parallel to the surface. Along the slope, the component of the weight down the slope (w sin θ) is balanced by the static friction force up the slope. Perpendicular to the slope, the component of the weight into the surface (w cos θ) is balanced by the normal force. The friction is STATIC because the block is not sliding — the question says it rests without moving. Static friction adjusts itself to whatever value is needed to prevent motion, up to a maximum; kinetic friction acts only once the surfaces are actually sliding over each other.
questions.explanation: Three conventions are marked in an NSC diagram and are worth more than they look. Every arrow STARTS at the body and points outwards — arrows drawn towards the body lose the mark even when the physics is right. The normal force is perpendicular to the SURFACE, not vertical, and on a slope those are different directions. And only forces acting ON the block belong on the diagram: the force the block exerts on the plank is a different force on a different body and does not appear. Note there are exactly three forces here, not four — "the component of the weight down the slope" is part of the weight, not an extra force, and drawing it as a fourth arrow is a common way to lose a mark.

memo.text: Normal force drawn perpendicular to the slope surface, labelled
Friction drawn up the slope, parallel to the surface, labelled
The weight component along the slope balanced by friction
Static friction, because the block is not sliding

questions.context: A person of mass 60 kg stands on a bathroom scale inside a lift. Take g as 9,8 m·s⁻². The lift accelerates upwards at 1,5 m·s⁻².
questions.prompt: Draw a labelled free-body diagram of the forces on the person, then calculate the reading on the scale and explain why it differs from the person’s weight.
questions.answer: Two forces act on the person: the normal force N from the scale, acting vertically upwards, and the weight w acting vertically downwards. The upward arrow is drawn LONGER than the downward one, because the person is accelerating upwards. Taking upwards as positive and applying Newton’s second law: N − w = ma, so N = m(g + a) = 60(9,8 + 1,5) = 60 × 11,3 = 678 N. The scale reads 678 N, whereas the person’s weight is mg = 60 × 9,8 = 588 N. It differs because a scale does not measure weight — it measures the NORMAL FORCE it exerts on whatever stands on it. When the lift accelerates upwards there must be a net upward force on the person, which requires the normal force to exceed the weight by exactly ma = 90 N. The person’s weight has not changed; only the support force has.
questions.explanation: The idea worth taking away is that a bathroom scale never measures weight, in a lift or anywhere else. It reads the normal force, which happens to equal the weight only when there is no vertical acceleration — which is why it works at all in an ordinary bathroom. The same reasoning gives the other cases directly: accelerating downwards makes N less than w, and in free fall N is zero, which is what "weightlessness" actually means. Drawing the arrows to different lengths is not decoration; it shows you have recognised a net force, and a diagram with equal arrows contradicts the answer that follows it.

memo.text: Normal force up and weight down, both labelled, drawn from the person
Upward arrow drawn longer, consistent with upward acceleration
Newton’s second law applied: N − w = ma
A scale reads the normal force, not the weight
