questions.context: A cell and a switch are connected in a single loop with resistor R₁. Two further resistors, R₂ and R₃, are connected in parallel with each other, and that parallel combination is in series with R₁. A learner must measure the current in the main line and the potential difference across the parallel combination.
questions.prompt: Draw a circuit diagram for this arrangement, showing where the ammeter and the voltmeter must be connected, and explain why an ammeter must have a very low resistance while a voltmeter must have a very high one.
questions.answer: The ammeter goes IN SERIES in the main line, between the cell and the rest of the circuit, so that the whole current passes through it. The voltmeter goes IN PARALLEL, with one lead at the point where the two branches divide and the other at the point where they rejoin, so that it is connected ACROSS the parallel combination. An ammeter must have a very low resistance because it is part of the path the current takes: any resistance it adds reduces the very current it is supposed to be measuring, so an ideal ammeter has zero resistance. A voltmeter must have a very high resistance because it is connected across a component and offers the current a second path: if it had low resistance a large part of the current would flow through the meter instead of through the component, changing the potential difference it is supposed to be measuring. An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance and draws no current at all.
questions.explanation: Both rules come from the same idea: a meter should tell you what the circuit was doing before you connected it. Series and parallel are not arbitrary conventions here — they follow from what each meter measures. Current is the same at every point along a series path, so to measure the current in the main line the meter has to sit in that path. Potential difference is a difference between two points, so the meter has to touch both points, which means connecting it across the component. The resistance requirements then follow: anything in the path must add as little as possible, and anything bridging two points must steal as little as possible.

memo.text: Cell, switch and R₁ in one series loop, correct symbols used
R₂ and R₃ drawn as two separate branches between the same two junctions
Ammeter in series in the main line
Voltmeter in parallel, across the parallel combination
Low ammeter resistance, so it does not reduce the current it measures
High voltmeter resistance, so it draws almost no current from the component

questions.context: VSEPR theory: electron pairs (bonding and lone) around a central atom arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible.
questions.prompt: Use VSEPR theory to determine and name the molecular shape of a methane molecule, CH₄.
questions.answer: Tetrahedral, with bond angles of approximately 109.5°.
questions.explanation: Carbon has 4 bonding pairs of electrons (one to each of the 4 hydrogen atoms) and no lone pairs. With 4 electron pairs and no lone pairs to repel unevenly, the pairs arrange themselves as far apart as possible in three dimensions, giving a symmetrical tetrahedral shape.

questions.context: Electronegativity values: H = 2.1; C = 2.5; O = 3.5; N = 3.0.
questions.prompt: Using the electronegativity values given, calculate the electronegativity difference for the C–O bond and for the C–H bond, and state which of the two bonds is more polar.
questions.answer: C–O difference = 1.0; C–H difference = 0.4. The C–O bond is more polar (it has the larger electronegativity difference).
questions.explanation: C–O: |3.5 − 2.5| = 1.0. C–H: |2.5 − 2.1| = 0.4. A larger electronegativity difference between the two bonded atoms indicates a more unequal sharing of the bonding electron pair, and hence a more polar bond.

questions.context: Approximate electronegativity-difference ranges: 0 to 0.4 = non-polar covalent; 0.4 to 1.7 = polar covalent; greater than 1.7 = ionic.
questions.prompt: Explain how the electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms can be used to classify a bond as non-polar covalent, polar covalent, or ionic, and classify a bond with an electronegativity difference of 2.1.
questions.answer: A very small electronegativity difference (roughly 0 to 0.4) indicates the bonding electrons are shared almost equally, giving a non-polar covalent bond. An intermediate electronegativity difference (roughly 0.4 to 1.7) indicates the bonding electrons are shared unequally, with the more electronegative atom attracting the shared pair more strongly, giving a polar covalent bond. A large electronegativity difference (greater than roughly 1.7) indicates the more electronegative atom effectively removes the electron entirely from the other atom, giving an ionic bond (rather than a shared pair at all). A bond with an electronegativity difference of 2.1 would be classified as ionic.
questions.explanation: This classification reflects a continuous spectrum of bonding character rather than three strictly separate categories: as electronegativity difference increases, electron sharing becomes progressively more unequal, until at a large enough difference the bond is better described as a full transfer of an electron (ionic) rather than an unequal sharing (polar covalent).

questions.prompt: Predict whether each substance dissolves well in water, using the rule "like dissolves like": (a) sodium chloride; (b) ethanol; (c) iodine (I₂); (d) hexane.
questions.answer: (a) Dissolves: ionic, attracted to polar water molecules. (b) Dissolves: polar, forms hydrogen bonds with water. (c) Hardly dissolves: non-polar molecules. (d) Does not dissolve: non-polar.
questions.explanation: Polar and ionic solutes dissolve in a polar solvent like water; non-polar solutes dissolve in non-polar solvents.

questions.prompt: Iodine dissolves readily in hexane but only slightly in water. Explain this difference in solubility in terms of intermolecular forces.
questions.answer: Iodine and hexane are both non-polar, held by London forces of similar strength, so iodine-hexane forces can replace the forces broken. Water molecules are held by strong hydrogen bonds, which iodine cannot replace, so little iodine dissolves.
questions.explanation: A solute dissolves when the new solute-solvent forces are comparable to those that must be broken.

memo.text: Iodine and hexane both non-polar (London forces)
Similar forces, so like dissolves like
Iodine cannot replace water’s hydrogen bonds

questions.prompt: Ethanol and water mix in all proportions. Explain this solubility by referring to the intermolecular forces in each liquid.
questions.answer: Both are polar and both have hydrogen bonds between their molecules (each has an –OH group). Ethanol molecules can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, which replace the ones broken, so they mix completely.
questions.explanation: Like dissolves like: two liquids with the same kind of intermolecular force mix readily.

memo.text: Ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with water
These replace the forces broken, so they mix

questions.context: pV = nRT; R = 8.31 J·K⁻¹·mol⁻¹
questions.prompt: A gas occupies a volume of 5 dm³ (0.005 m³) at a pressure of 202.65 kPa and a temperature of 298 K. Calculate the number of moles of gas present.
questions.answer: n ≈ 0.41 mol

questions.context: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ (constant temperature)
questions.prompt: A gas occupies a volume of 8 dm³ at a pressure of 100 kPa. Calculate the new volume of the gas if the pressure is increased to 200 kPa, at constant temperature.
questions.answer: V₂ = 4 dm³

questions.context: P₁V₁ ÷ T₁ = P₂V₂ ÷ T₂
questions.prompt: A gas occupies a volume of 4 dm³ at a pressure of 101.3 kPa and a temperature of 290 K. Calculate the volume of the gas at a pressure of 150 kPa and a temperature of 310 K.
questions.answer: V₂ ≈ 2.89 dm³

questions.context: A learner weighs out a sample of magnesium on a balance and records its mass as 4,00 g. The molar mass of magnesium is 24,3 g·mol⁻¹.
questions.prompt: Calculate, to the correct number of significant figures, the number of moles of magnesium in the sample.
questions.answer: n = m / M = 4,00 / 24,3 = 0,16460905… mol. Both measurements are given to three significant figures — 4,00 g has three (the two zeros after the comma are recorded digits, not padding) and 24,3 g·mol⁻¹ has three — so the answer is written to three significant figures: n = 0,165 mol.
questions.explanation: The rule for multiplying and dividing is that the answer carries as many significant figures as the LEAST precise value that went into it, and the reason is worth understanding rather than memorising: a calculated result cannot be more certain than the measurement it came from. Writing 0,16460905 mol claims the sample was weighed to eight significant figures, which the balance simply did not do. Note the trap in 4,00 g: trailing zeros after the decimal comma are significant, because the learner wrote them down to say the balance read zero in those places. Had the mass been recorded as 4 g it would have one significant figure and the answer would be 0,2 mol.

memo.text: Answer given to three significant figures, matching the data

questions.context: n = m ÷ M; M(NaCl) = 58.5 g·mol⁻¹
questions.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of sodium chloride (NaCl) present in an 11.7 g sample.
questions.answer: n = 0.20 mol

questions.context: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). Molar mass: Mg = 24 g·mol⁻¹; MgO = 40 g·mol⁻¹.
questions.prompt: Calculate the mass of magnesium oxide (MgO) produced when 6.0 g of magnesium reacts completely with oxygen.
questions.answer: mass MgO = 10.0 g
questions.explanation: n(Mg) = 6.0 ÷ 24 = 0.25 mol. Since the mole ratio of Mg to MgO is 2:2 (i.e. 1:1), n(MgO) = 0.25 mol. mass(MgO) = n × M = 0.25 × 40 = 10.0 g.

questions.prompt: For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, ΔH = -92 kJ·mol⁻¹. Is the reaction exothermic or endothermic? Compare the energy of the products with that of the reactants, and say what happens to the temperature of the surroundings.
questions.answer: Exothermic, because ΔH is negative. The products have less energy than the reactants; the difference is released, so the surroundings warm up.
questions.explanation: ΔH = energy of products − energy of reactants, so a negative value means energy was given out.

memo.text: Products have less energy than reactants

questions.prompt: For N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, ΔH = -92 kJ·mol⁻¹ (per 2 mol of NH₃ formed). Calculate the energy released when 3 mol of NH₃ is formed.
questions.answer: 92 kJ is released per 2 mol NH₃, so 3 mol releases 92 × 3/2 = 138 kJ.
questions.explanation: ΔH belongs to the balanced equation as written, so scale it by the number of moles actually formed.

questions.prompt: The thermal decomposition CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ has ΔH = +178 kJ·mol⁻¹. Calculate the energy needed to decompose 250 g of calcium carbonate (M = 100 g·mol⁻¹), and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
questions.answer: n = 250 ÷ 100 = 2,5 mol. Energy = 2,5 × 178 = 445 kJ absorbed. ΔH is positive, so the reaction is endothermic.
questions.explanation: An endothermic reaction must be supplied with energy continuously -- here by heating in a kiln.

questions.prompt: Define a redox reaction.
questions.answer: A redox reaction is a chemical reaction in which oxidation (loss of electrons) and reduction (gain of electrons) occur simultaneously.
questions.explanation: The name "redox" is a combination of "reduction" and "oxidation", reflecting that these two processes always occur together in the same reaction — one species cannot lose electrons unless another species gains them.

questions.prompt: Define an acid, according to the Arrhenius definition.
questions.answer: An Arrhenius acid is a substance that increases the concentration of hydrogen ions (H⁺) when dissolved in water.
questions.explanation: This is the simplest definition of an acid taught at this level; a more general definition (the Lowry-Brønsted definition, an acid as a proton donor) is used in later, more advanced treatments of acids and bases.

questions.prompt: For the reaction Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g), determine the oxidation number of zinc and hydrogen before and after the reaction, and identify the oxidising agent.
questions.answer: Zn: 0 → +2 (oxidised); H: +1 → 0 (reduced). Hydrochloric acid (HCl, via the H⁺ ion) is the oxidising agent.
questions.explanation: Zinc’s oxidation number increases from 0 to +2 (loses electrons, is oxidised); hydrogen’s oxidation number decreases from +1 to 0 (gains electrons, is reduced), making the H⁺ ions (supplied by HCl) the oxidising agent.

questions.prompt: A boat moves upstream at 3 m·s⁻¹ relative to the water, while the river flows downstream at 1,2 m·s⁻¹. Taking upstream as the positive direction, add the velocities to find the resultant velocity of the boat.
questions.answer: Resultant = (+3) + (−1,2) = +1,8 m·s⁻¹, so 1,8 m·s⁻¹ upstream.
questions.explanation: Give each vector a sign from the chosen positive direction, then add algebraically.

questions.prompt: A learner walks 25 m east, then 40 m west, then 10 m east. Taking east as positive, calculate the resultant displacement and the total distance walked.
questions.answer: Displacement = (+25) + (−40) + (+10) = −5 m, which is 5 m west. Distance = 25 + 40 + 10 = 75 m.
questions.explanation: Displacement is a vector, so directions cancel. Distance is a scalar, so every leg adds.

questions.prompt: In a tug-of-war, three learners pull to the left with forces of 520 N, 480 N, 610 N, and two learners pull to the right with forces of 700 N and 650 N. Taking right as positive, calculate the resultant force on the rope and state which way it will move.
questions.answer: Right: +1 350 N. Left: −1 610 N. Resultant = 1 350 + (−1 610) = −260 N. The negative sign means 260 N to the left, so the rope moves to the left.
questions.explanation: Fewer learners can still lose or win: it is the sum of the forces with their signs that decides.

questions.prompt: A car moving at 12 m·s⁻¹ accelerates uniformly at 2,5 m·s⁻² for 6 s. Use the equations of motion to calculate its final velocity and the distance it covers.
questions.answer: vf = vi + aΔt = 12 + 2,5 × 6 = 27 m·s⁻¹. Δx = viΔt + ½aΔt² = 12 × 6 + ½ × 2,5 × 6² = 117 m.
questions.explanation: List what is given (vi, a, Δt) and what is required before choosing each equation.

questions.prompt: A driver brakes and brings a car travelling at 25 m·s⁻¹ to rest in 50 m, with uniform acceleration. Use the equations of motion to calculate the acceleration and the time taken to stop.
questions.answer: vf² = vi² + 2aΔx: 0 = 25² + 2a(50), so a = −6,25 m·s⁻² (negative: against the motion). Δt = (vf − vi) ÷ a = (0 − 25) ÷ (−6,25) = 4 s.
questions.explanation: Taking the direction of motion as positive, a deceleration comes out as a negative acceleration.

questions.prompt: A ball is dropped from rest from a high balcony and falls freely for 2,5 s. Taking g = 9,8 m·s⁻², use the equations of motion to calculate its velocity after 2,5 s and the distance it has fallen.
questions.answer: vf = vi + gΔt = 0 + 9,8 × 2,5 = 24,5 m·s⁻¹ downwards. Δy = viΔt + ½gΔt² = ½ × 9,8 × 2,5² = 30,63 m.
questions.explanation: In free fall the acceleration is 9,8 m·s⁻² downwards; "dropped" means the initial velocity is zero.

questions.prompt: Explain why mechanical energy is not conserved when friction acts on a moving object, and state what happens to the energy that seems to be missing.
questions.answer: Friction converts some of the mechanical energy into heat (thermal energy) and sound, which are not part of mechanical energy. The energy is not destroyed: the total energy of the system is still conserved.
questions.explanation: Mechanical energy is kinetic plus gravitational potential energy only. Friction moves energy out of that total into forms the sum does not count.

memo.text: Friction converts mechanical energy into heat and sound

questions.prompt: A 2 kg box slides from rest down a rough ramp from a height of 1,5 m and reaches the bottom at 4 m·s⁻¹. Calculate how much mechanical energy friction converted to heat and sound.
questions.explanation: At the top: Ep = mgh = 2 × 9,8 × 1,5 = 29,4 J, and Ek = 0. At the bottom: Ek = ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 4² = 16 J, and Ep = 0. The difference, 29,4 − 16 = 13,4 J, is the energy friction converted to heat and sound.

questions.prompt: A 60 kg learner starts from rest at the top of a playground slide 3 m high. Friction converts 40% of her initial potential energy into heat and sound. Calculate her speed at the bottom of the slide.
questions.explanation: Ep at the top = 60 × 9,8 × 3 = 1 764 J. Only 60% of it becomes kinetic energy: Ek = 0,6 × 1 764 = 1 058,4 J. Then ½ × 60 × v² = 1 058,4, so v² = 35,28 and v = 5,94 m·s⁻¹.

questions.prompt: Two pulses with amplitudes of 3 cm and 2 cm travel towards each other on a rope. What is the amplitude of the resultant pulse when they meet if (a) both are crests, (b) one is a crest and the other a trough? Name the type of interference in each case.
questions.answer: (a) 5 cm, constructive interference  (b) 1 cm, destructive interference
questions.explanation: By the principle of superposition the displacements add. Crest + crest: 3 + 2 = 5 cm. Crest + trough: 3 + (−2) = 1 cm.

questions.prompt: Define constructive interference and destructive interference.
questions.answer: Constructive interference: two pulses (crests with crests, or troughs with troughs) overlap and their amplitudes add to give a larger pulse. Destructive interference: a crest overlaps a trough and the amplitudes subtract to give a smaller pulse.
questions.explanation: Both follow from the principle of superposition: the resultant displacement is the sum of the separate displacements.

questions.prompt: A crest and a trough of exactly the same amplitude and shape travel towards each other on a rope. Describe the rope at the instant the pulses exactly overlap, and what happens afterwards.
questions.answer: At that instant the rope is flat -- the resultant displacement is zero everywhere, complete destructive interference. Afterwards the two pulses emerge and continue in their original directions, unchanged, as if they had never met.
questions.explanation: The energy has not disappeared while the rope is flat: the rope is still moving. Pulses pass through each other and continue unchanged.

memo.text: Rope flat: zero displacement (complete destructive interference)
The pulses continue in their original directions

questions.prompt: A hammer strikes one end of a steel rail 1 700 m long. Sound travels at 5 000 m·s⁻¹ in steel and 340 m·s⁻¹ in air. Calculate how long the sound takes to reach the other end through each medium, and explain why a listener there hears two sounds.
questions.answer: Steel: t = 1 700 ÷ 5 000 = 0,34 s. Air: t = 1 700 ÷ 340 = 5 s. The sound through the steel arrives 4,66 s earlier, because particles in a solid are closer together and pass the vibration on faster.
questions.explanation: The same sound travels at different speeds in different media, so the two paths arrive at different times.

memo.text: Sound is faster in the solid
Closer particles pass the vibration on more quickly

questions.prompt: Sound travels faster in liquids than in gases: 340 m·s⁻¹ in air but 1 500 m·s⁻¹ in water. Explain, in terms of how close the particles are, why sound travels faster in the water, then calculate the wavelength of a 680 Hz sound in each medium.
questions.answer: The particles in a liquid are much closer together than in a gas, so each one passes the vibration to the next more quickly. λ = v ÷ f. In air: 340 ÷ 680 = 0,5 m. In water: 1 500 ÷ 680 = 2,21 m.
questions.explanation: The source sets the frequency; the medium sets the speed, so the wavelength changes in proportion to the speed.

memo.text: Water particles are closer together, so they pass the vibration on faster

questions.prompt: Rank steel, water and air from the medium in which sound travels fastest to the one in which it travels slowest, and explain the order in terms of the particles.
questions.answer: Steel, then water, then air. The particles are closest together in a solid and furthest apart in a gas, and closer particles pass the vibration on more quickly.
questions.explanation: Sound is a longitudinal wave passed from particle to particle, so its speed depends on how close and how strongly linked the particles are.

memo.text: Particles closest in solids, furthest apart in gases
Closer particles transmit the vibration faster

questions.prompt: What is ultrasound? Give TWO uses of ultrasound.
questions.answer: Ultrasound is sound with a frequency above 20 000 Hz, too high for humans to hear. Uses (any two): prenatal imaging of a baby, detecting flaws in metal, echolocation by bats and dolphins, sonar.
questions.explanation: The upper limit of human hearing is about 20 000 Hz; anything above it is ultrasound.

memo.text: Second use, e.g. detecting flaws in metal / echolocation

questions.prompt: A ship sends a pulse of ultrasound down to the sea floor. The echo returns 0,8 s later. The speed of sound in sea water is 1 500 m·s⁻¹. Calculate the depth of the sea.
questions.explanation: The pulse travels down to the sea floor and back up, so the total distance is v × t = 1 500 × 0,8 = 1 200 m. The depth is half of that: 600 m.

questions.prompt: A bat uses echolocation: it emits a pulse of ultrasound and hears the echo from a moth 0,02 s later. The speed of sound in air is 340 m·s⁻¹. How far away is the moth?
questions.explanation: The echo travels to the moth and back: total distance = 340 × 0,02 = 6,8 m, so the moth is 3,4 m away.

questions.prompt: Light behaves as a stream of photons. Calculate the energy of one photon of green light of frequency 5,5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (h = 6,63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
questions.explanation: Each photon is a packet of energy; its energy depends only on the frequency of the light.

questions.prompt: Blue light of wavelength 450 nm can be treated as a stream of particles (photons). Calculate its frequency, and then the energy of one photon using E = h f. (c = 3,0 × 10⁸ m·s⁻¹; h = 6,63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
questions.explanation: The wave equation gives the frequency; the photon model then gives the energy each packet carries. 450 nm = 4,5 × 10⁻⁷ m.

questions.prompt: Calculate how many times more energy a photon of ultraviolet light (1 × 10¹⁵ Hz) carries than a photon of radio waves (1 × 10⁸ Hz), and use the particle nature of light to say why only one of them can damage skin cells.
questions.answer: E is proportional to f, so the ratio is 1 × 10¹⁵ ÷ 1 × 10⁸ = 1 × 10⁷. Each ultraviolet photon carries enough energy to damage molecules such as DNA in a cell; a radio photon carries far too little, however many arrive.
questions.explanation: Damage depends on the energy of each photon, not the total amount of radiation.

memo.text: Each UV photon has enough energy to damage cells; a radio photon does not

questions.prompt: In paper chromatography, an unknown dye travels 3,6 cm while the solvent travels 8 cm. Calculate how far the dye travels as a fraction of the solvent (its Rf value), and decide whether it could be a known dye with an Rf value of 0,45 in the same solvent.
questions.answer: Rf = distance travelled by the dye ÷ distance travelled by the solvent = 3,6 ÷ 8 = 0,45. It matches the known dye’s 0,45, so the unknown could be that dye.
questions.explanation: Chromatography separates dissolved substances by how far they travel with the solvent. A substance always has the same Rf value in the same solvent, so matching values suggest the same substance.

memo.text: Matches: could be the known dye

questions.prompt: Which separation method recovers the pure solvent (water) from a salt solution?
questions.answer: Distillation
questions.explanation: Evaporation recovers the dissolved salt but lets the water escape. Distillation boils off the water and condenses it again, so the solvent is recovered.

questions.prompt: Describe, step by step, the separation methods you would use to recover sand, salt and iron filings from a mixture of all three.
questions.answer: First use a magnet: magnetism separates the magnetic iron filings. Then add water and stir, so the salt dissolves. Filtration then separates the insoluble sand, which stays in the filter paper. Finally, evaporation (or crystallisation) of the filtrate recovers the dissolved salt.
questions.explanation: Each method works on a different property: magnetism, solubility, particle size and boiling point.

memo.text: Evaporate the filtrate to recover salt

questions.context: A sealed syringe contains a fixed amount of gas at a constant temperature.
questions.prompt: Using the kinetic molecular theory, explain why the pressure of the gas increases when the plunger of the syringe is pushed in, decreasing the volume available to the gas.
questions.answer: Decreasing the volume forces the same number of gas particles into a smaller space. This means the particles collide with the walls of the syringe more frequently (per unit time and per unit area), which increases the pressure exerted by the gas. Since the temperature is constant, the average kinetic energy of the particles does not change.
questions.explanation: Pressure arises from the frequency and force of particle collisions with the container walls, which increases as particles are confined to a smaller volume.

questions.context: Solid carbon dioxide ("dry ice") changes directly into carbon dioxide gas at room temperature and atmospheric pressure, without passing through a liquid phase.
questions.prompt: Name this process, and use the kinetic molecular theory to explain why it occurs.
questions.answer: The process is called sublimation. Particles at the surface of the solid occasionally gain enough kinetic energy to completely overcome the (relatively weak) attractive forces holding them in the solid lattice, allowing them to escape directly into the gas phase without first forming a liquid, because a stable liquid phase for carbon dioxide does not exist under these particular conditions of temperature and pressure.
questions.explanation: Sublimation occurs because, for certain substances under certain conditions, particles can gain enough energy to jump directly from the solid to gas state.

questions.context: A sealed, rigid gas cylinder is left in direct sunlight and warms up.
questions.prompt: Using the kinetic molecular theory, explain why the pressure inside the cylinder increases as its temperature rises, while its volume stays constant.
questions.answer: As the temperature increases, the gas particles gain kinetic energy and move faster on average. This causes the particles to collide with the walls of the cylinder more frequently, and with greater force per collision, resulting in an increase in the pressure exerted by the gas. The volume remains constant because the cylinder is rigid and cannot expand or contract.
questions.explanation: Pressure depends on both the frequency and the force of particle collisions with the container walls, both of which increase with rising temperature.

questions.prompt: In the simple model of electron arrangement used for the first 20 elements, how many electrons can the second energy level hold?
questions.explanation: The first energy level holds 2 electrons and the second holds 8 (2 in the 2s orbital and 6 in the three 2p orbitals).

questions.prompt: A sodium atom has 11 electrons. Write its electron arrangement by energy level, and state how many valence electrons it has.
questions.answer: 2, 8, 1: two in the first energy level, eight in the second, and one in the third. It has one valence electron.
questions.explanation: Fill the lowest energy level first, then move upwards once each level is full.

questions.prompt: Explain why electrons fill the energy levels from the lowest upwards.
questions.answer: Electrons closest to the nucleus are held most strongly and have the lowest energy. An atom is most stable when its energy is as low as possible, so each electron occupies the lowest energy level that still has space.
questions.explanation: This is called the Aufbau principle: build up from the bottom.

memo.text: Lowest level has the lowest energy
Lowest energy is most stable, so they fill first

questions.prompt: Give the family name of the elements in group 1 and in group 17 of the periodic table (the alkali metals or the halogens), and the number of valence electrons in each group.
questions.answer: Group 1: the alkali metals, with one valence electron. Group 17: the halogens, with seven valence electrons.
questions.explanation: Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, which is why they react alike.

questions.prompt: Explain why the noble gases in group 18 are unreactive.
questions.answer: They have a full outer energy level, which is a stable arrangement, so they do not need to lose, gain or share electrons.
questions.explanation: Other atoms react to reach the full outer energy level the noble gases already have.

memo.text: Stable: no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons

questions.prompt: The alkali metals become more reactive down group 1. Explain why potassium reacts more vigorously with water than sodium does.
questions.answer: A potassium atom is larger than a sodium atom: its single valence electron is in an energy level further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons. It is held less strongly, so potassium loses it more easily and reacts more vigorously.
questions.explanation: The alkali metals react by losing their one valence electron; the easier it is to lose, the more reactive the metal.

memo.text: Potassium atom is larger; valence electron further from the nucleus
Electron lost more easily, so more reactive

questions.context: Electronegativity values: carbon (C) = 2,5; oxygen (O) = 3,5.
questions.prompt: Using the electronegativity values given, determine and explain the type of bond (non-polar covalent, polar covalent, or ionic) formed between a carbon atom and an oxygen atom.
questions.answer: The electronegativity difference is 3,5 − 2,5 = 1,0, which falls within the polar covalent range (approximately 0,4 to 1,7). The bond is therefore a polar covalent bond: the shared electron pair is not shared equally, with oxygen (the more electronegative atom) attracting the electrons more strongly, giving oxygen a partial negative charge and carbon a partial positive charge.
questions.explanation: The size of the electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms indicates whether the resulting bond is non-polar covalent, polar covalent, or ionic in character.

questions.context: Electronegativity values: nitrogen (N) = 3,0; hydrogen (H) = 2,1.
questions.prompt: Using the electronegativity values given, determine and explain the type of bond (non-polar covalent, polar covalent, or ionic) formed between a nitrogen atom and a hydrogen atom.
questions.answer: The electronegativity difference is 3,0 − 2,1 = 0,9, which falls within the polar covalent range (approximately 0,4 to 1,7). The bond is therefore a polar covalent bond: the shared pair of electrons is shared unequally, with nitrogen (the more electronegative atom) attracting the electron pair more strongly, giving nitrogen a partial negative charge and hydrogen a partial positive charge.
questions.explanation: The magnitude of the electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms indicates the type and degree of polarity of the resulting bond.

questions.context: As a general guideline: ΔEN < 0.4 → non-polar covalent bond; 0.4 ≤ ΔEN < 1.7 → polar covalent bond; ΔEN ≥ 1.7 → ionic bond, where ΔEN is the difference in electronegativity between the two bonded atoms.
questions.prompt: Using the electronegativity values given, classify the type of bond formed in EACH of the following, showing the electronegativity difference (ΔEN) used: (a) K (0.8) bonded to Br (2.8) (b) Si (1.8) bonded to O (3.5) (c) Cl (3.0) bonded to Cl (3.0).
questions.answer: (a) ΔEN = 2.0 → ionic bond  (b) ΔEN = 1.7 → ionic bond  (c) ΔEN = 0 → non-polar covalent bond
questions.explanation: (a) 2.8 − 0.8 = 2.0, which is ≥ 1.7, so the K–Br bond is ionic. (b) 3.5 − 1.8 = 1.7, which meets the ΔEN ≥ 1.7 guideline, so the Si–O bond is classified as ionic here. (c) 3.0 − 3.0 = 0, which is < 0.4, so the Cl–Cl bond is non-polar covalent, as expected between two atoms of the same element.

questions.prompt: For the reaction H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, breaking bonds absorbs 436 kJ for one mole of H–H bonds and 242 kJ for one mole of Cl–Cl bonds; making bonds releases 431 kJ for each mole of H–Cl bonds. Calculate the net energy change and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
questions.answer: Energy absorbed in breaking bonds = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ. Energy released in making bonds = 2 × 431 = 862 kJ. Net change = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ. More energy is released than absorbed, so the reaction is exothermic.
questions.explanation: Two moles of H–Cl bonds form, so the energy released is doubled. A negative net change means energy leaves the reaction to the surroundings.

memo.text: Exothermic: more released in making bonds than absorbed in breaking them

questions.prompt: When citric acid reacts with sodium hydrogen carbonate in a test tube, the temperature falls from 22 °C to 9 °C. State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and explain using the energy absorbed in breaking bonds and the energy released in making bonds.
questions.answer: Endothermic. More energy is absorbed in breaking the bonds of the reactants than is released in making the bonds of the products, so the reaction takes energy from its surroundings and the test tube feels cold.
questions.explanation: The thermometer measures the surroundings: a fall in temperature means energy has gone into the reaction.

memo.text: More energy absorbed in breaking bonds than released in making bonds

questions.prompt: Classify each of these reactions as exothermic or endothermic: (a) burning methane; (b) photosynthesis; (c) neutralising hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide; (d) the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate.
questions.answer: (a) Exothermic. (b) Endothermic. (c) Exothermic. (d) Endothermic.
questions.explanation: Combustion and neutralisation release energy; photosynthesis needs light energy and thermal decomposition needs heating.
